Daniel 9:24-27 is the most precise time prophecy in the Bible: seventy weeks, or sevens, decreed for Daniel's people and his holy city. How you count them shapes how you read the rest of Bible prophecy. This study walks through the text phrase by phrase, lets you run the count yourself, compares the four main ways of reading it, and then lays every major end-time passage on one timeline from Daniel's exile to the fall of Jerusalem. It follows the partial preterist reading: the seventy weeks reach their goal in Christ's first coming, and the desolation they announce fell in AD 70. The other views, their strongest points, and the objections to this reading are all set out fairly.

Every Christian view in this study holds that Daniel is true prophecy and that Christ will return bodily to raise the dead and judge the world. Partial preterism sees most of the prophecies about the end of the old covenant age fulfilled by AD 70, while Christ's second coming, the resurrection and the final judgement remain future, as the creeds confess. Full preterism, which places the resurrection and the return in the past, is outside the historic creeds and is not the view taught here.

The inserted gap

Daniel gives a single block: seventy weeks, divided 7 + 62 + 1. Placing nearly two thousand years between the 69th and 70th weeks adds something the text never mentions; no reader before the 19th century counted it that way as a system.
Count the weeks continuously and the Messiah appears at the 69th and is cut off in the 70th, as the text says.
The wrong “he”

In 9:26 “the prince who is to come” is not the subject; “the people” are. The person the whole passage is about is the Anointed One. Making “he” in 9:27 a future Antichrist skips the Messiah to reach a minor noun.
The Messiah confirms the covenant with many, as Jesus said of his blood “poured out for many.”
A covenant turned into a treaty
Nothing in the text speaks of a peace treaty or of breaking one. The word is covenant, and the verb means to make strong or confirm.
In Daniel 9, covenant is God's covenant (9:4). The Messiah confirms it.
Special pleading on the year
The 360-day “prophetic year” is used only when it makes the count fit 444 BC to AD 33. Israel's calendar added months to keep pace with the sun, so its years averaged 365 days.
A normal year count from 457 BC reaches AD 27 without adjustment.
Elastic “generation”
“This generation” is read literally in Matthew 23:36 (judgement on Jesus' hearers) but as “this race” or “the future generation” in 24:34, eleven verses later.
Read the same phrase the same way in both places.
Elastic “soon”

Revelation says its events “must soon take place” and “the time is near,” while Daniel was told to seal his book because the time was far off. Reading “near” as two thousand years reverses the contrast.
Daniel's distant visions became near in John's day.
Unfalsifiable double fulfilment
When a sign fits the first century, it is called a partial fulfilment with a greater one still to come. That makes any prophecy endlessly postponable and impossible to test.
Look for a fulfilment the New Testament itself names before adding a second one.
Newspaper exegesis
Reading today's news into the text, a form of the presentism fallacy, has produced failed predictions in every generation since the second century.
Begin with what the text meant to its first hearers.
A temple the text does not mention
Daniel 9 mentions only the temple that would be destroyed (9:26), which was the second temple. A third temple must be supplied from elsewhere.
The sanctuary of Daniel 9 is the one Titus burned.
A seven-year tribulation built from one verse
The seven-year tribulation rests on putting the 70th week in the future. Revelation never mentions a seven-year period, and no text places a rapture before it.
Revelation's numbers are 42 months, 1,260 days and “a time, times and half a time”: half of a week, not a whole one.
The miscounted prophecy
Dating the seventy weeks from 587 to 164 BC gives about 423 years, so the critical view must say the author got his own number wrong.
A count that reaches the Messiah exactly is a better explanation than an author who miscounted.
Ruling out prophecy in advance
The late dating of Daniel often begins from the assumption that detailed prediction is impossible. That decides the question before the evidence is weighed.
Jesus calls Daniel a prophet and treats his abomination as still future in AD 30.
Precision dissolved
The text divides the weeks into 7, 62 and 1 and places events after the 62. A purely symbolic count cannot explain why such divisions are given.
The divisions mark real stages: rebuilding, waiting, and the Messiah's week.
Everything already past
Full preterism places the resurrection and Christ's return in AD 70, but Paul condemns those who say the resurrection has already happened.
Partial preterism keeps the bodily return and resurrection future.

Eusebius (c. 325) applied Matthew 24 to AD 70 at length, as did Chrysostom.

Preterists see the fulfilment of Daniel 9 and Matthew 24 as one of the strongest proofs that Scripture is true.
Preterists make everything symbolic.
They take the time words literally and read symbols as apocalyptic language, as the prophets used it.
They read “soon,” “near” and “this generation” plainly, and the cosmic imagery as the prophets' language for the fall of nations (Isaiah 13:10).

What is a “week” in Daniel 9?
A unit of seven: here seven years. Seventy weeks are 490 years.

The Hebrew word means a seven. Daniel had been reading Jeremiah's seventy years of exile (9:2), and Gabriel answers with seventy sevens: seven times longer, echoing the sabbath-year laws of Leviticus 25-26, where neglected sabbath years brought exile. The exile lasted seventy years; the full restoration would take seventy weeks of years.
Leviticus 25:8: seven weeks of years, forty-nine years, to the jubilee.
2 Chronicles 36:21: the land kept its sabbaths seventy years.
Daniel 10:2 adds “days” when it means weeks of days.
Symbolic readers take the sevens as round periods rather than exact years.
Who are “your people” and “your holy city”?
Daniel's people, Israel, and Jerusalem. The weeks set the time left for them before the Messiah comes and the old order ends.

Gabriel tells Daniel the seventy weeks are decreed for Israel and Jerusalem. Within that time the Messiah would come, deal with sin and confirm the covenant; and because the city rejected him, it would be destroyed. The partial preterist reading sees the prophecy entirely kept in that history. Dispensationalists agree it concerns Israel and therefore leave the church age out of the count.
Daniel 9:16-19: Daniel prays for your city and your people.
Luke 19:42-44: Jesus weeps that Jerusalem did not know the time of its visitation.
Dispensationalists hold that because the prophecy concerns Israel, its last week must wait for God to resume his program with the nation.
Were all six goals of Daniel 9:24 fulfilled?
Yes. Each describes what Christ accomplished: sin ended, atonement made, everlasting righteousness brought in, prophecy sealed and the Most Holy anointed.

The six goals are not political; they are about sin and righteousness. The New Testament says Christ put away sin by his sacrifice once at the end of the ages, made atonement, revealed God's righteousness, and was anointed with the Spirit. The checklist on this page pairs each goal with the verse that says it was done.
Hebrews 9:26: once at the end of the ages to put away sin.
Romans 3:21-25: the righteousness of God revealed; Christ the propitiation.
Acts 10:38: God anointed Jesus with the Holy Spirit.
Dispensationalists say “everlasting righteousness” and the end of Israel's transgression await the nation's repentance at Christ's return.
Who is the Anointed One who is “cut off”?
Jesus the Messiah, crucified. Almost all Christian views agree.

After the sixty-two weeks an anointed one would be cut off and have nothing. The word is used of being killed (Genesis 9:11). Isaiah says the Servant was “cut off out of the land of the living” (53:8). Jesus was crucified around AD 30, about three and a half years into his ministry, in the middle of the seventieth week.
Isaiah 53:8: cut off out of the land of the living.
John 2:13; 6:4; 11:55: three Passovers in John's Gospel, suggesting a ministry of over three years.
Critical scholars identify the anointed one as the high priest Onias III, murdered in 171 BC.
Where does the count begin?
With a word to restore and build Jerusalem. The best candidates are 457 BC (Ezra) and 444 BC (Nehemiah).

Four decrees are proposed: Cyrus (538), Darius (520), Artaxerxes to Ezra (457) and Artaxerxes to Nehemiah (444). Cyrus' decree is about the temple. The 457 decree restored the city's legal and civic life and funded its restoration; Ezra 9:9 already speaks of a wall. The 444 commission rebuilt the walls. Try each one in the calculator on this page.
Ezra 7:25-26: appoint magistrates and judges.
Ezra 9:9: to give us a wall in Judea and Jerusalem.
Nehemiah 2:5: send me to the city, that I may rebuild it.
Dispensationalists prefer 444 BC because Nehemiah's commission explicitly concerns the city's walls.
Should the years be 365 days or 360?
Israel's calendar kept pace with the sun by adding a month when needed, so its years averaged about 365 days. The 360-day year is needed only for the 444 BC count.

Revelation equates 1,260 days with 42 months, which some take as proof of 30-day months and 360-day years. But that is a symbolic half-week, not a calendar rule. Jewish years were lunar months adjusted to the solar year by an extra month, as the festivals had to fall at harvest time. Counting normal years from 457 BC reaches AD 27.
457 BC + 483 years = AD 27 (there is no year 0).
444 BC + 483 years of 360 days (about 476 solar years) = AD 33.
Dispensationalists argue that Genesis 7-8 (150 days for five months) shows 30-day months in prophetic reckoning.
Why is the first period seven weeks?
The first forty-nine years cover the rebuilding of the city “in a troubled time,” from Ezra and Nehemiah to the end of the Old Testament era.

Gabriel says the city would be rebuilt with squares and moat, but in a troubled time. Ezra and Nehemiah record opposition, and Malachi, the last prophet, wrote in this period. After that came sixty-two weeks of waiting with no new prophet, until John the Baptist and Jesus.
Nehemiah 4:17: each worked with one hand and held a weapon with the other.
Luke 16:16: the Law and the Prophets were until John.
Critical scholars place the seven weeks from 587 to 538 BC, ending with Cyrus.
When did the seventieth week end?
About AD 34, seven years after Jesus' baptism, when the gospel moved beyond Jerusalem to Samaria and the Gentiles after Stephen's death.
